## Sub-change 1: the field declaration ([Document.ts:316-322](server/models/Document.ts#L316-L322))

```ts
@Length({
  max: DocumentValidation.maxArchivedReasonLength,
  msg: `Archived reason must be ${DocumentValidation.maxArchivedReasonLength} characters or less`,
})
@Column(DataType.TEXT)
@SkipChangeset
archivedReason: string | null;
```

Each decorator does a distinct job, stacked on the same property:
- **`@Length`** — a Sequelize-validator hook that runs on `save()`. It's the DB-layer half of the length enforcement we discussed earlier (paired with the API schema's `.max()`), reading the same shared constant so the two can't drift.
- **`@Column(DataType.TEXT)`** — tells Sequelize this property maps to the actual `archivedReason` column we added in the migration, typed as unbounded text (not `STRING`, which Postgres caps around 255 chars by convention — `TEXT` matches what the migration declared).
- **`@SkipChangeset`** — excludes this field from "changeset" tracking. Changesets are how this codebase computes diffs of a document's *content* (used for revision history / collaborative editing). `archivedReason` is administrative metadata about an action taken on the document, not part of its body — without `@SkipChangeset`, setting this field could get swept into content-diffing logic that has nothing to do with it. I mirrored this exactly from how `summary` (the line just above it, [Document.ts:308-314](server/models/Document.ts#L308-L314)) is decorated, since it's the same kind of thing: free-text, user-facing, not document content.

`string | null` (not just `string`) reflects reality: most documents were never archived, so this is `null` for the overwhelming majority of rows, and becomes `null` again after unarchiving (sub-change 3).

## Sub-change 2: threading `reason` through the archive call chain ([Document.ts:1206](server/models/Document.ts#L1206), [:1413](server/models/Document.ts#L1413))

```ts
archiveWithCtx = async (ctx: APIContext, reason?: string) => {
  ...
  await this.archiveWithChildren(ctx, reason);
  return this;
};

private archiveWithChildren = async (ctx: APIContext, reason?: string) => {
  ...
  this.archivedReason = reason ?? null;
  ...
};
```

This is two edits, not one, because `archiveWithCtx` is the *public* method the API route calls, but it doesn't do the actual archiving itself — it handles removing the document from its collection's structure, then delegates the real work to the *private* `archiveWithChildren`, which is the method that recursively walks and archives child documents. The parameter has to be added to **both** signatures because `archiveWithCtx` is just a pass-through here: it receives `reason` from the route handler and has to hand it down to the method that actually does the `this.archivedReason = ...` assignment. Skip either one and the value gets dropped somewhere in the middle — e.g., if I'd only added it to `archiveWithChildren`, `archiveWithCtx` would have no way to receive it from the caller in the first place.

The `reason ?? null` at the assignment site matters too: `reason` is `string | undefined` (an optional param, meaning "not provided" is `undefined`), but the column is typed `string | null`. Postgres/Sequelize wants `null` for "no value," not `undefined` — so this normalizes "caller didn't pass anything" into the correct empty representation for the database.

**Why only the directly-archived doc, not children:** `archiveWithChildren`'s inner `archiveChildren` recursive helper ([Document.ts:1420-1434](server/models/Document.ts#L1420-L1434)) sets `child.archivedAt = archivedAt` for every descendant, but I deliberately did **not** add `child.archivedReason = reason` there. If you archive a parent document with 10 nested children, all 11 documents get `archivedAt` set (they're all now "archived" in the sense of being hidden/moved), but only the parent — the one the user actually took the action on and typed an explanation for — gets the reason. Setting the same reason on every child would be misleading noise: "Superseded by the new onboarding doc" written on the parent doesn't mean each of its 10 sub-pages individually deserves that exact same explanation attached to them; it's really a statement about the parent's role, and the children just went along for the ride because they're nested under it.

## Sub-change 3: clearing on unarchive ([Document.ts:1404-1410](server/models/Document.ts#L1404-L1410))

```ts
await restoreChildren(this.id);
this.archivedAt = null;
this.archivedReason = null;
this.lastModifiedById = user.id;
this.updatedBy = user;
this.collectionId = collectionId;
return this.saveWithCtx(ctx, undefined, { name: "unarchive" });
```

Without this line, restoring an archived document back to active use would leave the *old* explanation sitting on the row even though the document is no longer archived. Picture the sequence: archive with reason "Outdated, replaced by v2" → someone later decides that was wrong and unarchives it → without this fix, the document is now active again but still silently carries "Outdated, replaced by v2" in its `archivedReason` field. If it then gets re-archived *without* typing a new reason (the field is optional), the stale text from the first archiving would still be sitting there, now attached to a completely different archive event, showing an explanation that doesn't correspond to why it was archived *this* time. Clearing it here keeps the field meaning exactly one thing: "the explanation for the current archive, if any" — never a leftover from history.

## Why all three live in `Document.ts` rather than, say, the route handler

This is the point of the "why" I gave originally: `archiveWithCtx`, `archiveWithChildren`, and `restoreArchivedWithChildren` are already where every other piece of archive/unarchive business logic lives (removing from collection structure, cascading to children, setting `archivedAt`, logging the event). Putting the `archivedReason` rules here — not just "storage exists" but the *rules* about when it's set and when it's cleared — keeps one coherent method responsible for what "archiving" and "unarchiving" actually mean, rather than splitting that logic between the model and the route handler (which should stay a thin translator between HTTP and the model, per this codebase's own convention of "keep API routes thin, use model methods for business logic").

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-16 20:42:09Z)**_

## The change, in full

```ts
export const DocumentsArchiveSchema = BaseSchema.extend({
  body: BaseIdSchema.extend({
    /** An optional explanation for why the document is being archived */
    reason: z
      .string()
      .max(DocumentValidation.maxArchivedReasonLength)
      .optional(),
  }),
});
```

Before this, `body` was just `BaseIdSchema` directly — a fixed object with a single `id` field. `.extend({...})` takes that base shape and adds one more field to it, so the request body is now `{ id, reason? }` instead of just `{ id }`.

## What each piece is doing

- **`z.string()`** — declares the type. If a client sent `reason: 123` (a number) or `reason: { text: "..." }` (an object), Zod rejects the request with a `400` before any application code runs. This is the first line of defense against malformed input.
- **`.max(DocumentValidation.maxArchivedReasonLength)`** — caps the length at 1000 characters, using the same shared constant the model's `@Length` validator reads (the "single source of truth" point from a few turns back). If someone sent a 5000-character reason, Zod rejects it here, at the API boundary, before it ever reaches the database.
- **`.optional()`** — this is the piece that makes the field backward-compatible. It means the schema accepts a request *with* `reason` present, but is equally happy with a request that omits it entirely. Without `.optional()`, Zod would require every caller to include `reason`, which would break the existing frontend action flow (the `archiveDocument` action from `app/actions/definitions/documents.tsx` currently calls `document.archive()` with no reason at all, and step 3 — the dialog — hasn't been built yet). Marking it optional means old callers and new callers can coexist.

## Where this sits in Zod's evaluation order, and why that matters

Zod schemas run as **middleware**, before the route handler function executes at all — that's what the `validate(T.DocumentsArchiveSchema)` line does in the route registration ([server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts:1416](server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts#L1416)). So the sequence for a request is:

1. Request arrives at `POST /api/documents.archive`.
2. `validate(T.DocumentsArchiveSchema)` runs Zod against the body. If `reason` is the wrong type, or over 1000 characters, the request is rejected right here with a `400` — the route handler function never even starts running.
3. Only if validation passes does execution reach the handler, where `const { id, reason } = ctx.input.body;` destructures the now-validated, now-typed values.

This is why the schema change had to come before (or alongside) the route handler change: without it, even if the handler tried to read `ctx.input.body.reason`, TypeScript wouldn't know that property exists on the inferred request type (`DocumentsArchiveReq`, generated by `z.infer<typeof DocumentsArchiveSchema>` on the last line), because the schema is also what generates the *type* the handler code is checked against. Extending the schema does two jobs simultaneously: it's both the runtime guard that rejects bad input, and the compile-time contract that makes `reason` a recognized, correctly-typed field (`string | undefined`) anywhere `DocumentsArchiveReq` is used.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-16 20:59:20Z)**_

Yes — `z.string()` accepts any string of text. That's exactly what it's for. So a real request like:

```json
{ "id": "abc123", "reason": "Superseded by the new onboarding doc" }
```

passes `z.string()` without issue — `"Superseded by the new onboarding doc"` is a string, so it's accepted, then checked against `.max(1000)` (also passes, since it's well under 1000 characters), then flows through as the `reason` the user actually typed.

What `z.string()` rejects is anything that **isn't** a string at all — the type check happens before the content of the text is even considered:

| Sent value | Passes `z.string()`? |
|---|---|
| `"Superseded by v2"` | ✅ yes — this is exactly the normal case |
| `""` (empty string) | ✅ yes — technically a string, just empty |
| `123` | ❌ no — it's a number, not a string |
| `true` | ❌ no — boolean |
| `{ "text": "..." }` | ❌ no — an object |
| `["a", "b"]` | ❌ no — an array |
| `null` | ❌ no (unless you also add `.nullable()`, which I didn't — it's just `.optional()`, meaning the field can be *absent*, not explicitly `null`) |

So my earlier phrasing was probably confusing — I was only pointing out what gets rejected (malformed, non-text data), not implying `z.string()` is somehow choosy about *which* text it accepts. Any plain text the user types into the eventual archive-reason dialog will sail through `z.string()` fine; it only exists to guard against a client sending the wrong *shape* of data, not against ordinary text content.

## The change itself

```diff
- const { id } = ctx.input.body;
+ const { id, reason } = ctx.input.body;
  ...
- await document.archiveWithCtx(ctx);
+ await document.archiveWithCtx(ctx, reason);
```

Two edits in the same function: pull `reason` out of the request body alongside `id`, then pass it as the second argument to `archiveWithCtx`. On its own this is a trivial-looking two-line change, but it's the **hinge** of the whole feature — the one place where "a value that arrived over HTTP" turns into "a value passed to the business-logic layer." Everything before it in the request lifecycle exists to make this line possible; everything after it exists because of what this line does.

## What it depends on (upstream)

1. **`ctx.input.body` having a `reason` property at all** — that only exists because of the schema change from a few turns ago. `ctx.input.body` is typed as `DocumentsArchiveReq`, which is `z.infer<typeof DocumentsArchiveSchema>`. Before that schema was extended, TypeScript would have flagged `const { id, reason } = ctx.input.body` as an error — `reason` wouldn't exist on the inferred type, so the compiler itself would block this line from being written correctly. The schema isn't just a runtime gate; it's what makes this destructuring type-check.
2. **Validation having already run** — `validate(T.DocumentsArchiveSchema)` at [line 1416](server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts#L1416) executes as middleware *before* this handler function runs at all (Koa middleware chain: `auth()` → `validate(...)` → `transaction()` → handler). By the time execution reaches `const { id, reason } = ctx.input.body`, `reason` is guaranteed to be either `undefined` or a string under 1000 characters — the handler never has to defend against a malformed `reason` itself, because bad input never makes it this far.
3. **`archiveWithCtx` accepting a second parameter** — the destination of the forwarded value, `document.archiveWithCtx(ctx, reason)`, only compiles because the model method's signature was changed to `archiveWithCtx = async (ctx: APIContext, reason?: string) => {...}` (the earlier `server/models/Document.ts` change). If that signature still only accepted `ctx`, passing a second argument wouldn't cause a TypeScript error (JS/TS allow calling with extra args), but the value would be silently discarded — `archiveWithCtx` simply wouldn't have a parameter name bound to it, so nothing downstream would ever see it.
4. **`authorize(user, "archive", document)` at [line 1428](server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts#L1428)** — this line didn't change, but it's a dependency in the sense that it still gates the whole operation: whatever `reason` says, the user still has to be permitted to archive this specific document before any of this executes. Adding a `reason` field didn't introduce a new authorization concern (it's not sensitive data, just an explanation string), so no changes were needed here — but it's worth noting explicitly *why* it wasn't touched: the ability check is about the *action* (archiving), not the *shape* of its payload.

## What depends on it (downstream)

1. **The actual database write.** Inside `archiveWithCtx` → `archiveWithChildren`, the line `this.archivedReason = reason ?? null;` only receives a real value because this route handler forwarded one. If this handler still called `archiveWithCtx(ctx)` with no second argument, `reason` inside the model method would always be `undefined`, and `archivedReason` would always end up `null` — the column and validators would all still "work," but the feature would be silently inert end-to-end.
2. **The presenter's output.** `presentDocument(ctx, document)` at [line 1433](server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts#L1433) reads `document.archivedReason` off the in-memory model instance *after* `archiveWithCtx` has run and set it. Because `document` is the same object being mutated and saved earlier in this same function, the response sent back to the browser reflects the just-saved value without needing a second database round-trip.
3. **Everything on the frontend side (steps 3–4, not yet built).** The eventual archive dialog will need to actually send `reason` in its `POST` body for any of this to matter — but that's only possible *because* the server now knows what to do with it if it arrives. In other words: the frontend work is meaningful precisely because this handler is now ready to receive and use what it sends.

So this change is the fulcrum: it's short because it's mostly just "receive a value, then hand it off" — but it's the exact point where the request-validation side (schema) and the business-logic side (model) get wired together, and nothing on either side of it does anything useful without this connection existing.

## The change

```diff
  archivedAt: document.archivedAt,
+ archivedReason: document.archivedReason,
  deletedAt: document.deletedAt,
```

One line, added right next to `archivedAt` — deliberately placed there so the two travel together in the payload as a pair.

## What a "presenter" actually is, and why this line has to exist

`presentDocument` is the **translation layer** between "a Sequelize model instance living in server memory" and "the JSON object that actually gets sent over HTTP to the browser." This is a deliberate architectural boundary in this codebase (AGENTS.md explicitly calls it out: *"Use presenters to format API responses"*) — the frontend never receives a raw Sequelize model. It receives exactly and only the fields listed in this `res` object.

That distinction matters here specifically: **having `archivedReason` on the Sequelize model does not mean the frontend can see it.** `document` (the parameter to this function) is a full model instance — at this point in the code, `document.archivedReason` is already sitting there in memory with whatever value was just saved by `archiveWithCtx`/`archiveWithChildren`. But nothing about that fact makes it appear in the HTTP response. The `res` object is built field-by-field, explicitly — if a property isn't named here, it's simply absent from the JSON the client gets back, no matter what the underlying model holds.

## What it depends on (upstream)

1. **`document.archivedReason` existing as a real, populated field on the model** — this only has a meaningful value because of the whole earlier chain: the migration created the column, the model declared the field, the route handler forwarded `reason` into `archiveWithCtx`, and that method set `this.archivedReason = reason ?? null` before saving. If any one of those links were missing, this line would still "work" (no TypeScript error, no crash) — it would just always present `null`.
2. **The property name matching exactly.** `document.archivedReason` has to be spelled identically to the `@Column` field name declared in `server/models/Document.ts:322`. TypeScript's type-checking on `Document` catches this for us — if I'd mistyped it as `document.archiveReason` (missing the `d`), this wouldn't compile at all, because `Document` has no such property. That's actually a nice safety net this presenter file benefits from just by being TypeScript.

## What depends on it (downstream)

1. **The immediate archive response.** Back in the route handler ([documents.ts:1432-1435](server/routes/api/documents/documents.ts#L1432-L1435)), `ctx.body = { data: await presentDocument(ctx, document), ... }` — this is the payload sent back to whoever just called `POST /documents.archive`. Without this line in the presenter, that response would include `archivedAt` but no `archivedReason`, even though the reason was correctly saved to the database seconds earlier.
2. **Every other place this same document gets fetched later.** `presentDocument` isn't only called from the archive route — it's the shared presenter used whenever a document is serialized to JSON anywhere in the API (viewing a document, listing archived documents, etc., since `presentDocument` is a common shared entry point). Adding it here means `archivedReason` becomes visible everywhere a document is presented, not just in the direct response to the archive action itself. That's exactly what's needed for the eventual Archive-list page (step 4): when a user loads `/archive` later — possibly in an entirely new browser session, possibly a *different* user on the team — the `documents.archived` API call runs through this same presenter, and only because `archivedReason` is listed here does that response include the explanation at all.
3. **The frontend model.** Once this reaches the browser as JSON, `app/models/Document.ts` (not yet updated — that's part of the still-pending frontend step) will need an `archivedReason` field to receive it into. But that step is only meaningful because the server is now actually sending the value — there'd be nothing for the frontend model to receive otherwise.

So this one line is the **exit door** for the value: everything before it (migration → model field → schema → route handler) exists to get `reason` *into* the document; this line is what lets it back *out* to anyone who asks the API about that document afterward.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-16 21:54:58Z)**_

## The test, in full

```ts
it("should persist and return an archive reason when provided", async () => {
  const admin = await buildAdmin();
  const user = await buildUser({ teamId: admin.teamId });
  const collection = await buildCollection({
    userId: user.id,
    teamId: user.teamId,
  });
  const document = await buildDocument({
    userId: admin.id,
    teamId: user.teamId,
    collectionId: collection.id,
  });
  const res = await server.post("/api/documents.archive", user, {
    body: {
      id: document.id,
      reason: "No longer relevant to the current project",
    },
  });
  const body = await res.json();
  expect(res.status).toEqual(200);
  expect(body.data.archivedReason).toEqual(
    "No longer relevant to the current project"
  );
});
```

## Setup: building a realistic scenario, not a mock

The first four lines (`buildAdmin`, `buildUser`, `buildCollection`, `buildDocument`) are test-fixture factories that create **real rows in the actual test Postgres database** — this codebase's test suite doesn't mock the database, it exercises the real Sequelize models against a real (test) instance. I copied this setup verbatim from the existing `"should allow archiving document"` test right above it ([documents.test.ts:4279-4300](server/routes/api/documents/documents.test.ts#L4279-L4300)), rather than inventing my own — same admin/user/collection/document scaffolding, so the two tests are directly comparable and either could be extended by someone reading the pair.

- `buildAdmin()` — creates a team and an admin user (needed because `buildDocument` below is created by this admin).
- `buildUser({ teamId: admin.teamId })` — a second, regular user on the same team; **this is who performs the archive action**, not the admin.
- `buildCollection(...)` — a collection the document lives in, since a document normally belongs to one.
- `buildDocument(...)` — the actual document under test, authored by the admin but sitting in a collection the regular `user` has access to.

## The request: exercising the real HTTP route

```ts
const res = await server.post("/api/documents.archive", user, {
  body: { id: document.id, reason: "No longer relevant to the current project" },
});
```

`server.post` sends an actual HTTP POST through the test server, authenticated as `user`, hitting the real Koa route — meaning this request travels through the **entire chain** we've discussed over the last several turns: `auth()` middleware → `validate(DocumentsArchiveSchema)` (the schema change) → the route handler (`const { id, reason } = ctx.input.body`) → `document.archiveWithCtx(ctx, reason)` (the model change) → `presentDocument` (the presenter change). This is deliberately an integration test of the whole round trip, not a unit test of any single layer in isolation — which is exactly why it belongs in `documents.test.ts` (this file exercises the API routes) rather than, say, a narrower test on `Document.ts` alone.

## The assertions: what "worked" actually means here

```ts
expect(res.status).toEqual(200);
expect(body.data.archivedReason).toEqual("No longer relevant to the current project");
```

- **`res.status` is `200`** — confirms the request wasn't rejected anywhere along the chain. If the schema had a bug and rejected valid input, this would be a `400` and the test would fail here, before even reaching the second assertion.
- **`body.data.archivedReason` equals what was sent** — this is the actual point of the test. `body.data` is the JSON returned by `presentDocument`. For this to equal the input string, *every* link in the chain had to work correctly in sequence: the schema had to let the value through validation, the route handler had to read it off the body and forward it (not drop it), `archiveWithCtx`/`archiveWithChildren` had to actually assign `this.archivedReason = reason`, the database write had to succeed, and the presenter had to include `archivedReason` in its output. A failure in *any single one* of those five links — say, if I'd forgotten the presenter line from two turns ago — would make this exact assertion fail, since `body.data.archivedReason` would come back `undefined` instead of the expected string.

## What this test does *not* cover (and why that's fine for now)

- It doesn't test the length cap (`.max(1000)`) — a follow-up test could send a 1001-character reason and assert a `400`.
- It doesn't test that unarchiving clears the reason (`restoreArchivedWithChildren`'s `this.archivedReason = null` line) — that would need a second test that archives, unarchives, and checks the field is back to `null`.
- It doesn't test that child documents don't inherit the reason — that would need a test with a parent/child document pair.

I kept this one focused on the core round trip specifically because it's the thing that *all* of the individually-explained changes contribute to — it's the test that would have caught a mistake in any of the last several turns' worth of changes, which is exactly the coverage worth having before moving on to the frontend steps.
